12860:
Prolixity is the quality of using far more words than are needed to say something. It is the state of being unnecessarily long-winded — of padding out a message with so much extra detail, repetition, or digression that the actual point gets buried, delayed, or lost entirely. When someone or something has prolixity, they use ten sentences where two would do perfectly well.

The key word here is unnecessarily. Prolixity is not just about being long. It is about being long without good reason — length that serves the speaker more than the listener, and that tests the reader's patience rather than rewarding it.
What It Really Means in Practice

Imagine you ask a colleague, "Did the meeting go well?"

A normal person says: "Yes, it went really well."

A person guilty of prolixity says: "Well, you know, I was thinking about that on the way in this morning, actually, and I wasn't sure how it would go, because last time we had a meeting like this, things got a bit complicated, but I have to say, all things considered, and keeping in mind everything we discussed beforehand, which I think really helped set the tone, it actually went, and I say this with some confidence, pretty well, yes."

The answer — yes, it went well — is in there. But it is wrapped in so many unnecessary layers of thought, qualification, and side-commentary that it becomes exhausting to extract. That exhausting, unnecessary excess is prolixity.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Prolixity is not a neutral word. It carries a note of criticism and mild disapproval. When you say a piece of writing suffers from prolixity, you are not complimenting it for being detailed or thorough. You are saying it is bloated — that the writer did not respect the reader's time enough to trim it down.

It suggests:

  • Tedium (the reader or listener grows bored or weary)
  • Lack of discipline (the writer couldn't cut what needed cutting)
  • Obscured clarity (the core message is harder to find than it should be)

So prolixity is always a flaw, never a virtue.
An Important Distinction: Prolixity vs. Depth

This is a nuance that many learners miss, so pay attention here.

A long book is not automatically prolific with prolixity. A detailed scientific paper is not automatically a example of prolixity. A comprehensive explanation — like this one — is not prolixity, as long as every part of it genuinely serves the reader's understanding.

Prolixity = length without purpose.
Depth = length with purpose.

If a word, sentence, or paragraph earns its place by adding meaning, clarity, or necessary context, it is not prolixity. Prolixity is specifically the excess that could be removed without losing anything of value. Think of it like fat on a cut of meat — some fat adds flavour and is worth keeping, but prolixity is the part that is purely waste.

Prolixity is a formal word. You will encounter it mostly in:

  • Literary or book criticism — "The novel's prolixity in its middle chapters slows the story to a crawl."
  • Academic writing — "The report's prolixity made it difficult to identify the key recommendations."
  • Formal feedback or editing — "Please revise this section; its prolixity will frustrate the reader."
  • Descriptions of speakers — "His prolixity in meetings was legendary — a five-minute update always became forty-five."

You would not typically say to a friend, "Your prolixity is annoying me." That would sound stiff and unusual. In casual speech, people say wordiness, rambling, or going on and on. Prolixity belongs to more elevated, written, or formal contexts.

Since you want full ownership of this word, here are its close relatives:

  • Prolix (adjective) — the describing form. "He is a prolix writer." (meaning: he writes with prolixity)
  • Prolixly (adverb) — "She explained the matter prolixly." (meaning: in a wordy, rambling way)
  • Prolixity (noun) — the quality or state itself. "The prolixity of the contract confused everyone."

These words orbit the same idea as prolixity, and knowing them sharpens your understanding of exactly what prolixity means:

  • Verbosity — perhaps the closest synonym; excessive use of words in general
  • Wordiness — the everyday, informal way to say the same thing
  • Long-windedness — emphasises the exhausting, drawn-out quality
  • Garrulousness — excessive talkativeness specifically in speech (prolixity can apply to both speech and writing)
  • Loquacity — very talkative, though this can sometimes be neutral or even charming, unlike prolixity

• Brevity — shortness; using only as many words as are needed (often praised as a virtue)
  • Conciseness — expressing things fully but in a tight, trim way
  • Succinctness — brief and clearly expressed
  • Terseness — very brief, sometimes even to the point of seeming blunt

A writer praised for brevity is the opposite of one criticised for prolixity.

Here are several example sentences showing how prolixity is naturally used, from different angles:

  1. The professor's lectures were fascinating in theory, but their prolixity meant students lost focus long before he reached his main point.
  2. The legal document ran to sixty pages — a monument to prolixity — when ten pages would have said the same thing far more clearly.
  3. She was aware of her own prolixity and made a conscious effort to say less.
  4. The editor returned the manuscript with a single note: "Prolixity throughout. Cut by a third."
  5. His emails were notorious for their prolixity; reading one felt like wading through tall grass to find a single flower.
One Final Anchor to Lock It In

Here is a simple mental image to cement this word forever:

Imagine a garden hose with too much water pressure. The water (your message) is perfectly good — but it's coming out in such an overwhelming, sprawling, uncontrolled flood that instead of neatly watering the plant (the listener), it just soaks everything and leaves a mess. Prolixity is the excess water. A good writer or speaker controls the pressure — they deliver exactly as much as is needed, no more.

In short: prolixity = the quality of saying something in far more words than necessary, to the point of being tedious. It is always a criticism, applies to both writing and speech, and is the direct enemy of clarity, brevity, and the reader's patience.
12861:
A prologue is a separate opening section that comes before the main body of a story, play, film, or other creative work. Think of it as a "before we begin" moment — the author or storyteller steps in first to say something important, and then the actual story starts.

If a story were a stage play, the prologue would be what happens before the curtain rises on Act One.
What Does a Prologue Actually Do?

A prologue serves a specific purpose — it is not just a fancy first chapter. It does one or more of the following things:

It gives you background you need before the story begins. Some stories are set in a complicated world, or involve events that happened long ago. Instead of awkwardly stuffing that context into Chapter 1, the author puts it in a prologue so you walk into the story already equipped.

It sets the mood and tone. A prologue can create a feeling — of mystery, danger, wonder, or sadness — so that you're in the right emotional state before the main story takes over.

It shows a moment in time that is separate from the main story. This is very common. A prologue might show you a scene from 200 years before the story takes place, or even a glimpse of the future. It's like a flash of light from a different time, placed at the very beginning.

It introduces a narrator or a key voice. Sometimes a character steps forward in the prologue to directly address the reader or audience and frame the story for them. Shakespeare did this often in his plays — a character called "Chorus" would deliver a prologue to prepare the audience.

Imagine a novel about a war. The story itself follows a young soldier in the 1940s. But the novel opens with a prologue — a short scene where an old man, sitting alone in a quiet room decades later, picks up a photograph and whispers, "It was never supposed to end this way."

Then the prologue ends. Chapter One begins, and we're back in the 1940s.

That prologue did something powerful. It told you: someone survives this war. Someone grows old. But something went wrong. Now you carry that weight as you read every chapter that follows. The prologue prepared you emotionally and intellectually before the story even started.
A Prologue Is Its Own Separate Thing

This is important: a prologue is distinct from Chapter One. It stands apart. It often has its own label — literally the word "Prologue" written at the top — and it is understood to exist outside the main flow of the narrative. If you removed it, the story would still make sense; but without it, you might feel slightly lost, or you'd miss something the author wanted you to feel from the very first page.
How a Prologue Differs from Similar Things

Prologue vs. Preface / Introduction: A preface or introduction is used in non-fiction books (like textbooks or memoirs). It is usually the author speaking directly to the reader in their own real-world voice, explaining why they wrote the book. A prologue, by contrast, belongs to fiction and drama — it is part of the creative, storytelling world of the work.

Prologue vs. Epilogue: These two are perfect opposites. A prologue comes at the beginning; an epilogue comes at the end. If a prologue is the "before," the epilogue is the "after." Many works have both — they frame the story like bookends on a shelf.

Prologue vs. First Chapter: A first chapter is the story beginning. A prologue is before the story begins. The first chapter introduces the story's present world; a prologue often introduces something outside that world — a different time, a different perspective, or essential context.

"Prologue" is also used in a broader, figurative sense in everyday language — meaning anything that comes before and leads into something bigger.

For example:

  • "The small border skirmishes were a prologue to the full-scale war that followed."
  • "Her early experiments in painting were merely a prologue to the masterpieces she'd create later in life."

In these cases, "prologue" is being used metaphorically. The speaker is saying: that earlier thing was not the main event — it was the introduction to the main event.

A prologue is an opening section that comes before the main story begins, used to provide background, set the tone, or show a moment in time separate from the central narrative — and more broadly, it refers to anything that serves as an introduction or lead-up to something greater that follows.
12862:
To prolong something means to make it last longer than it would have naturally, normally, or originally been planned to last. You are stretching something out in time — pulling its ending further into the future.

Think of it this way: imagine a candle that would naturally burn out in one hour. If you do something to make it burn for two hours instead, you have prolonged its life.
The golden rule about this word

You can only prolong something that is already happening or already exists. You cannot prolong something that has not started yet. Prolong is always about an ongoing situation, experience, condition, or state — and you are making it continue longer than it otherwise would.
The feeling and tone of the word

"Prolong" most often appears in one of two situations:

When someone deliberately chooses to make something last longer. A doctor prolongs a patient's life. A speaker prolongs a speech. A chef adds preservatives to prolong a food's shelf life.

When something unintentionally or unwantedly causes a situation to drag on. A storm prolongs a journey. A bad decision prolongs a conflict.

Because of this, the word frequently carries a slightly negative or serious tone — especially when it appears with words like suffering, pain, agony, or war. In those cases, making something last longer is obviously bad. But prolong is not an inherently negative word. You can just as naturally prolong a pleasant vacation, a beautiful musical note, a comfortable silence, or a happy moment. The tone depends entirely on what is being prolonged.

These examples show the word used across different situations so you can feel exactly how it works:

  • The doctors worked tirelessly to prolong the patient's life. — A deliberate, positive act of extending how long someone lives.
  • Stop prolonging the meeting — we need to make a decision and go home. — Used negatively; the meeting is going on longer than it should.
  • Heavy traffic prolonged our journey by nearly two hours. — Something external caused a trip to last longer than expected.
  • She kept asking questions to prolong the conversation, not yet ready to say goodbye. — A deliberate, emotionally motivated act.
  • Refusing to face the problem will only prolong your suffering. — A warning: avoiding something makes the bad situation last even longer.
  • Adding salt to water slightly prolongs the time it takes to boil. — A practical, neutral, scientific usage.
  • The peace negotiations were prolonged by disagreements over minor details. — Used in the passive voice; something caused the negotiations to go on longer.

Notice in that last example how "prolong" works in the passive voice too — the negotiations were prolonged by something. This is very common. The thing doing the prolonging can be a person, a decision, a substance, a circumstance, or an event.

Also notice: prolong always needs an object. You never say "it prolonged" on its own — you always prolong something. It is a transitive verb.
A crucial distinction: Prolong vs. Delay

These two words are easy to confuse, but they describe fundamentally different things.

Delay means to push back the start of something. The thing has not begun yet, and now it will begin later than planned.

Prolong means to extend the duration of something. The thing has already begun, and now it will end later than planned.

A simple illustration: if a surgery was scheduled for 9 AM but the surgeon arrives late and it begins at 11 AM, the surgery was delayed. But if the surgery was expected to take two hours and it ends up taking four hours in the operating room, the surgery was prolonged.

One word is about when something starts. The other is about how long it lasts. They are not interchangeable.
Common phrases and expressions you will encounter

"Prolong life / prolong someone's lifespan" — to help a person, animal, or even a machine or object survive or function longer than expected. This is one of the most common uses.

"Prolong suffering / prolong pain" — to make a painful experience last longer, usually used as a reason not to do something. ("Keeping him on that treatment will only prolong his suffering.")

"Prolong the agony" — a very common everyday expression meaning to make a painful, uncomfortable, or suspenseful situation last longer than necessary. It is often used with a touch of informal exasperation. ("Just tell me the result — stop prolonging the agony!")

"Prolong the inevitable" — to delay something bad that is certain to happen in the end no matter what. The word inevitable here means something that cannot be avoided. ("Staying in that failing business is just prolonging the inevitable.") This is a very widely used phrase, and it always carries the sense that all the prolonging is ultimately pointless.

"Prolong" sits comfortably in the middle of the formality scale. It fits naturally in everyday writing, news reporting, medical discussions, scientific explanations, and academic essays. It is not stuffy or overly academic — a person can use it in normal conversation without sounding strange. In very casual speech, people sometimes replace it with phrases like drag out or stretch out ("stop dragging this meeting out"), but prolong is never wrong or too formal for any situation.
The complete picture in one sentence

To prolong something is to deliberately or unintentionally make an ongoing thing last longer than it naturally or originally would have — and the word works equally well whether that extended duration is welcome, neutral, or regrettable.
12863:
Before you can understand "prom queen," you need to understand what a prom is, because the word "queen" only makes sense in that context.

A prom (short for promenade, a French word meaning a formal walk or parade) is a big, formal dance party held by high schools in the United States and Canada. Think of it as the grandest, most special event of a student's high school life. It is usually held near the end of the final year of high school, when students are around 17–18 years old.

Students dress up in elegant clothes — girls typically wear long gowns, and boys wear suits or tuxedos. They arrive in decorated cars or limousines, eat a fancy dinner, dance together in a beautifully decorated venue like a ballroom or hotel, and celebrate the near-end of their school years. It is a deeply sentimental, once-in-a-lifetime occasion for most American teenagers.

A prom queen is a female student who is voted by her peers (fellow students) to be the most popular and admired girl at the prom. She is essentially given the title of the "queen" of the event — the most celebrated female student of the night.

Here is how it works:

  • Before the prom, the school holds a vote. Students nominate and then vote for which girl (and which boy) they believe deserves the title.
  • A small group of finalists — called "prom queen nominees" or "the prom court" — are selected first based on the votes.
  • At the prom itself, during a special ceremony, the winner is announced in front of everyone.
  • The chosen girl is then crowned — meaning someone places a sparkling tiara (a small decorative crown) on her head in front of the whole school.
  • She is also typically given a bouquet of flowers, a sash (a ribbon worn across the shoulder that says "Prom Queen"), and loud applause from the crowd.

The prom king is the male equivalent — the most popular boy, crowned alongside her. Together, they are regarded as the "royal couple" of the night, and they usually share the first dance of the evening in front of everyone.

The title of prom queen is not based on grades, talent, or achievements. It is purely based on social popularity — how well-liked, admired, or socially influential a girl is among her classmates.

In traditional American high school culture, the prom queen was seen as the girl who had it all:

  • Physically attractive by conventional standards
  • Socially confident and outgoing
  • Well-connected — friends with many people, part of the "popular crowd"
  • Often a cheerleader, athlete, or student leader

Winning the title was considered one of the highest social honors a high school girl could receive. It was a public confirmation from the entire student body that she was the most admired girl in school.

In American culture, the prom queen is more than just a title — it is a symbol. It represents the peak of social success during the teenage years. For decades, American movies, TV shows, books, and songs have used the prom queen as a cultural shortcut to describe a certain type of person.

When someone calls a person a "prom queen" outside of an actual prom setting, they usually mean:

  • She was the most popular girl in school
  • She was beautiful and socially dominant in her youth
  • She represented the ideal of teenage social success in a traditional, mainstream sense

For example, if someone says "She was the prom queen back in high school," they are painting a picture of someone who was at the top of the social ladder during her teenage years.

Over time, especially in movies and TV, the prom queen became a well-known stereotype — a recurring character type with a very specific personality:

  • Pretty and popular, but sometimes vain or shallow
  • The center of attention, often surrounded by a group of followers
  • Socially powerful — capable of influencing who is accepted and who is left out
  • Sometimes portrayed as mean or unkind, especially to those less popular

You see this character in countless Hollywood films. In many stories, she is actually the antagonist (villain) — the popular girl who looks perfect on the outside but is cruel underneath. This version of the prom queen has become a classic trope (a repeated, recognizable character pattern) in teenage stories.

However, in other stories, she is portrayed more fairly — as a girl who is genuinely kind and deserving of her popularity.

The tradition of crowning a prom queen dates back to the early-to-mid 20th century in the United States, roughly the 1920s–1950s, when formal school dances became a widespread tradition. It was modeled loosely on the older concept of beauty queens — women crowned at pageants like the famous Miss America competition (which began in 1921).

As American high school culture grew and became more organized, schools began adding the crowning ceremony to make proms feel more special and memorable. The tradition spread widely and became a deeply embedded part of American teenage life by the 1950s and 1960s.

The prom queen tradition has faced significant criticism in modern times:

1. It reinforces shallow values. Critics argue that voting for a "queen" based on popularity teaches young people that looks and social status matter more than character, intelligence, or kindness.

2. It can be exclusionary. Students who are outsiders, shy, or simply not part of the popular crowd feel invisible or even hurt by the tradition, which highlights social hierarchies.

3. It is traditionally gendered. The concept of a "queen" has historically been limited to girls, which excludes non-binary students and reinforces rigid gender roles.

Because of these criticisms, many American schools have changed or eliminated the tradition. Some schools now crown a "prom court" without specific king/queen titles. Others allow students of any gender to run for either title. Some have dropped the crowning tradition altogether.
How It Is Used in Everyday Language

The term "prom queen" has traveled far beyond the walls of high schools and is used figuratively (not literally) in everyday conversation and media in several ways:

  • As a compliment or neutral description: "She was the prom queen type — gorgeous, confident, always surrounded by friends."
  • As a mild insult or criticism: "Don't worry about what she thinks — she's just acting like a prom queen." (Implying someone is arrogant or obsessed with status.)
  • Nostalgically: "Back in high school, she was prom queen. Now she works at the same grocery store as the rest of us." (Often used to describe how peak popularity in youth doesn't always translate to later life success.)
  • In song and pop culture: Countless songs, movies, and TV shows reference the prom queen. Examples include the song "Prom Queen" by various artists, movies like Carrie (1976) — a dark horror story about a prom queen election gone wrong — and TV shows like Glee, Euphoria, and Riverdale, all of which explore or satirize the concept.

AspectWhat It Means

In short:

  • A prom is a formal dance held at the end of high school in North America.
  • A prom queen is the girl voted most popular by her classmates, who is publicly crowned at the event.
  • The title symbolizes the peak of teenage social popularity.
  • As a cultural term, "prom queen" describes someone who was — or acts like — the most admired, attractive, and socially dominant girl in a high school setting.
  • The tradition has roots in early 20th-century American culture and has been both celebrated and criticized.
  • Today, the term is used both literally (to refer to the actual school tradition) and figuratively (to describe a personality type or social status).

Understanding "prom queen" gives you a window into a fascinating piece of American culture — one that reflects how teenagers navigate popularity, identity, beauty, and belonging during some of the most formative years of their lives.
12864: A promenade is about leisurely, unhurried movement through a public space — either as an activity (the act of walking) or as a place (a path built for walking). Think of it as the opposite of rushing somewhere. A promenade is slow, calm, and purposeful in its casualness.
Meaning 1: A Leisurely Walk in a Public Place

A promenade is a slow, relaxed walk taken in a public area, done for pleasure, fresh air, or simply to enjoy one's surroundings. It isn't about getting from point A to point B quickly. The journey is the point.

What makes a promenade different from just "a walk" is its social and public nature. Historically, and even today, people go on a promenade to enjoy being out in the world — to see the scenery, to be around other people, or simply to be seen themselves. There's a certain grace and ease to it.

Example: "The elderly couple took their evening promenade along the waterfront."
Meaning 2: A Place Designed for Walking

A promenade is also a specific type of path or wide walkway, usually in a public area, that is built or set aside for people to stroll along comfortably. It tends to be:

  • Wide and paved, so many people can walk side by side
  • Located somewhere scenic or pleasant — most commonly along a seafront, beach, riverbank, park, or boulevard
  • Often lined with benches, lampposts, railings, trees, or shops

This is the physical, architectural sense of the word. When a town or city has a "promenade," it usually refers to this grand, open walkway — a place that invites you to slow down.

Example: "The seaside promenade was packed with tourists enjoying the ocean breeze."

The two meanings connect naturally: a promenade (the place) is where you go for a promenade (the walk).
Meaning 3: A Formal Dance or Ball ("The Prom")

In another important sense, a promenade refers to a formal dance event, especially one held for students (typically at the end of a school year). This is where the word "prom" comes from — it is simply a shortened form of promenade.

The connection to the original meaning makes sense: at traditional formal balls and dances, guests would begin the evening by walking or parading through a grand hall to be introduced, seen, and admired by others — a literal promenade as an opening ceremony.

Today, the word "prom" carries almost all of this meaning in everyday speech (especially in American English), but the full word "promenade" is still used in formal or classical contexts when referring to a grand dance event.

Example: "The students arrived at the promenade in rented suits and elegant gowns."
Meaning 4: A Dance Figure or Movement

In certain types of partner dancing — like square dancing, ballroom dancing, and country dancing — a promenade is a specific, recognised movement or figure where couples walk together in a defined pattern, typically side by side or in a circle around the dance floor.

It is an instruction, a step, a choreographed moment — not just casual walking. When a caller in square dancing shouts "promenade!", it means the couples must walk around the set in a particular way.

Example: "The dancers completed the promenade before returning to their starting positions."
How All the Meanings Tie Together

Notice the golden thread running through every single meaning: a graceful, unhurried movement through a shared space, often with a sense of display or social presence.

Whether it's a path by the sea, an evening stroll, a school dance, or a movement in choreography — a promenade always carries a sense of elegance, leisure, and being present in public life. It is never rushed. It is never private. It belongs to open spaces and shared moments.

SenseWhat it means
ActivityA slow, leisurely walk in a public place
PlaceA wide, scenic public walkway (often by the sea)
EventA formal dance or ball (shortened to "prom")
Dance moveA specific walking figure in partner or folk dancing
12865: Prominence is the state of being easily noticed, standing out, or being well-known. The word captures the idea of being in front — not hidden, not in the background, but visible and recognized.

This is by far the most common use. When someone has prominence, they are well-known and respected — often within a specific field, profession, or community. A scientist might achieve prominence in her field after years of groundbreaking research. A politician gains prominence when the public and media start paying serious attention to them.

Importantly, prominence is not exactly the same as fame. A person can be prominent in a small town without being nationally famous. A judge can have enormous prominence in the legal world without most ordinary people knowing their name. Prominence is about being notable within a relevant circle or sphere, whereas fame is about being known by the general public at large.

It's also not the same as power. Someone can be powerful but operate in secrecy — they would lack prominence. Prominence requires visibility.
2. A physical thing that sticks out or projects

In a more literal, physical sense, a prominence is a part of something that juts out or rises above its surroundings. A rocky ledge sticking out from a cliff face is a prominence. A bump or raised feature on a surface can be called a prominence.

In astronomy, "solar prominences" are large, bright streams of plasma that arc out from the surface of the Sun — they literally "stick out" from it.
Key nuances that sharpen your understanding

• Prominence can be narrow in scope. You can have prominence in your neighborhood, in a particular industry, or across an entire country. It always helps to ask: prominent among whom?
  • Prominence is usually earned gradually. People rise to prominence — the phrase itself tells you it's a journey upward, not something you receive overnight.
  • Prominence is about being seen and known, not about your internal worth. A brilliant but unknown scientist lacks prominence, even if their work is extraordinary. Prominence is external — it lives in how others perceive and recognize you.
  • Prominence is neutral, not inherently positive. If a villain becomes widely known and feared, we might say they "gained prominence" — but the word itself doesn't celebrate them. It simply describes the fact that they are being noticed and recognized.
  • "Of prominence" = of high standing. You'll often read phrases like "a figure of great prominence" or "a matter of prominence," which simply mean a highly notable person or an important issue.

• Rise to prominence — to gradually become well-known or important in some area
  • National / international prominence — being known and notable at a national or global level
  • Give prominence to something — to highlight it, to make it more visible or important (e.g., "The newspaper gave prominence to the story by placing it on the front page.")
  • A position of prominence — a role or place where one is highly visible and respected
  • Achieve / gain prominence — to reach a state of being widely recognized

Think of prominence as a spotlight. When the spotlight is on you — when people are watching, noticing, and recognizing you — you have prominence. When that spotlight is off, you may still be talented or important in reality, but you lack prominence. The word always points to visibility and recognition, whether that means standing tall in a social or professional world, or literally sticking out above a surrounding surface.
12866:
Prominent means standing out — something that is easy to notice because it rises above, projects beyond, or is more important than the things around it.

Think of it as the opposite of blending in.
The Three Ways It Is Used

1. Physically sticking out

When something physically projects outward from a surface or from its surroundings, it is prominent.

"He had a prominent nose."
"The cliff had a prominent rocky ledge jutting out over the sea."
"Her prominent cheekbones gave her face a strong, defined look."

Here, prominent means the feature protrudes or stands out from the rest. You could replace it with "jutting out" or "noticeable because it sticks out."

2. Easily seen — in a conspicuous position

Something is prominent when it is placed or situated in a way that makes it impossible to miss.

"They put the warning sign in a prominent position at the entrance."
"The scar was prominent on his left cheek."
"The hotel stood in a prominent location on the hill, visible for miles."

Here, prominent is about visibility and placement. The thing is not hidden or tucked away — it's front and centre, drawing attention naturally.

3. Important and well-known (about people or things in society)

This is the most commonly used sense of the word. A prominent person is someone who is well-known, respected, and carries significant influence in their field or in society.

"She is a prominent lawyer in the city."
"He comes from a prominent family."
"The university published research by several prominent scientists."
"Poverty remains a prominent issue in the region."

Here, prominent means the person or thing has risen above the crowd in terms of reputation, importance, or influence. They are not just known — they are recognized and regarded by many people.
The Single Idea Connecting All Three Senses

All three meanings share one root idea: standing out above or beyond what is around it.

  • A prominent nose stands out from the face.
  • A prominent sign stands out from its surroundings.
  • A prominent person stands out from the crowd.

Once you grasp this core idea — standing out in a way that is hard to ignore — all uses of the word will feel natural to you.

• It does not mean the absolute best or number one. A prominent scientist is well-known and respected, but they are not necessarily the greatest scientist in the world.
  • It does not mean loud or aggressive. Something can be prominent in complete silence — like a prominent star in the night sky.
  • It does not mean temporary fame. Prominent suggests an established, recognized status, not a brief moment of attention.
  • It does not carry a negative meaning on its own. A prominent scar is simply very visible — the word itself does not say whether that is good or bad.

Prominent sits in the mid-to-high range of importance or noticeability. It is stronger than "noticeable" or "known," but not as extreme as "world-famous" or "the most important." Think of it as comfortably above average in recognition or visibility.

You can also intensify or soften it:

  • "a very prominent figure" — strongly stands out
  • "a fairly prominent mark" — stands out, but moderately
Close Words and How They Differ

Notable means worth paying attention to, but doesn't necessarily imply the same level of public recognition as prominent.

Eminent specifically refers to people who have earned an exceptionally high standing in their profession, often through years of achievement. It is narrower and more formal than prominent.

Conspicuous means very easy to see and often carries a slightly uncomfortable edge — as if the thing is too visible, awkwardly so. Prominent is more neutral and often positive.

Protruding / jutting out only covers the physical sense. Prominent covers all three senses.
Common Collocations (Words That Often Go With "Prominent")

These are the most natural word pairings:

  • prominent figure — an important, widely known person
  • prominent role — a major, clearly visible role or position
  • prominent position — a high-status job, or a location easy to see
  • prominent feature — a striking, noticeable characteristic
  • prominent member — a well-known and respected part of a group
  • prominent place / location — somewhere easily seen or highly valued
  • prominent issue — a major concern that many people are aware of
  • prominent display — shown in a place or manner that draws attention
Prominent means something or someone that clearly stands out — whether physically (projecting outward), visually (easy to spot), or socially (well-known and important).
12867: "Promiscuous" means not selective — engaging with many things or people without care, discrimination, or restriction. The single idea running through every use of this word is: no filter, no boundaries, accepting or doing things indiscriminately.

In everyday modern conversation, "promiscuous" almost always refers to a person who has many sexual partners, casually and without commitment or selectivity.

When someone is called promiscuous, it means they sleep with many different people, often without forming deep emotional bonds, and without being choosy about who those partners are.

Examples:

  • "He had a promiscuous lifestyle in his twenties."
  • "The novel's protagonist was a promiscuous woman who refused to be tied down."

This use carries a judgmental tone — calling someone promiscuous is rarely neutral. In most social contexts, it functions as mild to strong criticism, implying a lack of moral restraint or emotional depth. Historically, it was applied far more harshly to women than to men, and that double standard still lingers in how the word is perceived.

Before the sexual meaning became dominant, and still used today in more formal or literary writing, "promiscuous" simply means indiscriminate, randomly mixed, or carelessly unsorted — applied to anything, not just people or sexuality.

The idea is the same: no careful selection, no discrimination, everything jumbled together or accepted without distinction.

Examples in this sense:

  • "She was a promiscuous reader — she devoured detective novels, philosophy textbooks, and celebrity gossip with equal enthusiasm." (She read without any selectivity.)
  • "The aid was distributed in a promiscuous manner, with no real system for deciding who received what." (Aid was handed out indiscriminately.)
  • "The garden had a promiscuous beauty — wildflowers, weeds, and roses growing together in glorious disorder." (Mixed together without order.)
A Technical Use: "Promiscuous Mode" in Networking

In computer networking, a network card in promiscuous mode accepts all data packets passing through a network — even those not addressed to it. Normally, a network card filters and only accepts packets meant for it. In promiscuous mode, that filter is removed; it accepts everything indiscriminately.

This is a perfect illustration of the word's core meaning: no selectivity, no discrimination — accepting everything.

ContextTone
  • Used about a person's sexual behavior: Usually negative or judgmental, even if the speaker intends it clinically.
  • Used in literary/formal writing about non-sexual things: Neutral to slightly negative — implies sloppiness or lack of care.
  • Used in technical contexts (networking): Completely neutral and descriptive.

The word is not casual or slang — it's a formal, educated word. You'd encounter it more in books, essays, journalism, and formal speech than in casual everyday conversation.

No matter where you see "promiscuous" used, ask yourself: Is something happening without selection, without care, without discrimination? If yes, that's the word at work.

  • A promiscuous person doesn't discriminate in choosing sexual partners.
  • A promiscuous reader doesn't discriminate in choosing books.
  • A promiscuous distribution of resources doesn't discriminate in deciding who gets what.
  • A network card in promiscuous mode doesn't discriminate in deciding which data packets to accept.

One word, one idea: no filter.

• It's an adjective, so it describes nouns: a promiscuous person, promiscuous praise, promiscuous mixing.
  • Don't use it as a verb or noun — you'd say "promiscuity" (noun) or "promiscuously" (adverb).
  • Be aware: in most everyday contexts, people will assume you're talking about sexual behavior unless the context makes another meaning obvious.
  • It's a somewhat strong word. If you use it about a real person's sexual life, expect it to land as a criticism.
12868: The word promise has two distinct meanings as a noun. Both are common, and both are important to understand fully.
Meaning 1 — A commitment made to another person

A promise is a serious statement in which you tell someone that you will (or will not) do something in the future. When you make a promise, you are giving that person your word — meaning they have every right to trust and depend on what you said.

Three things define every promise in this sense:

It is directed at someone. You don't make a promise in the abstract; you make it to a specific person or group. You are the one making it, and someone else is on the receiving end.

It is always about the future. A promise is a commitment about something that will (or will not) happen later. You cannot promise something that has already occurred.

It creates an obligation. The moment you make a promise, you are morally and socially expected to follow through. This is what makes a promise different from a simple plan or intention. If you say "I will probably call you," that is an intention — soft and uncertain. If you say "I promise I will call you," you have created an obligation. The other person is now depending on you. You are responsible.

This sense of obligation is why breaking a promise — failing to do what you committed to — is considered a moral failure in nearly every culture. It damages trust and harms relationships. A promise is a bond of trust between two people.

A promise can be positive or negative. You can promise to do something ("I promise I'll be there") or promise to refrain from doing something ("I promise I won't tell anyone").

A promise can also be made to yourself. When you silently decide that you are going to hold yourself to something, that is a promise to yourself — "She made a promise to herself that she would never settle for less than she deserved."

Common phrases you will encounter (Meaning 1)

Make a promise — to commit to doing something
"He made a promise to call her every week."

Keep a promise — to honor what you said; to actually do the thing you committed to
"She always keeps her promises, no matter how hard it is."

Break a promise — to fail to do what you committed to; to not keep your word
"He broke his promise and never paid the money back."

Fulfill a promise — similar to "keep," but used especially for important, large, or long-standing commitments
"After years of delay, the government finally fulfilled its promise to build the school."

Go back on a promise — to abandon a promise you initially seemed to be honoring; often carries a sense of betrayal
"She went back on her promise at the last moment."

Extract a promise from someone — to get someone to commit to something, sometimes through pressure or persistence
"His mother extracted a promise from him that he would write every week."

Hold someone to their promise — to insist that a person does what they said they would do
"I'm going to hold you to that promise."

A promise is a promise — a common saying meaning that once you have committed to something, you are bound by it, regardless of how inconvenient it has become
"I know you don't want to go anymore, but a promise is a promise."

How serious is a promise? How does it compare to similar words?

A promise carries genuine moral weight, but how much weight depends on how it is made and in what context. "I promise I'll text you later" is relatively light. "I give you my solemn promise" is very heavy.

The English language has several words for different kinds of promises, each with a different level of seriousness and formality:

A vow is the most solemn kind of promise — deeply serious and often made in a religious or ceremonial setting. Wedding vows and a monk's vow of silence are classic examples. Vows are not easily broken, and breaking one is considered a very grave act.

An oath is a formal, usually public promise, often sworn on something important or sacred — a holy book, the constitution, one's honor. Taking an oath in court or swearing an oath of office are examples. It is institutional and carries legal or civic weight.

A pledge is also formal and often public, but usually made to a group, an institution, or a cause rather than to an individual. A politician's election pledge or a student pledging loyalty to their school are examples.

A guarantee is more transactional and less personal. In a guarantee, there is usually a specified consequence if the commitment is broken — your money back, a replacement item. It is common in business and commerce.

A promise, compared to all of these, sits in a comfortable middle ground. It is more personal and relational than a guarantee, more everyday and informal than an oath or vow, and more intimate than a pledge. It is the word you use between people who trust each other.
Meaning 2 — Signs of future potential or success

This is a completely different meaning of the same word, and it is equally common. When someone or something shows promise or holds promise, it means they display early signs that they could become excellent, valuable, or successful in the future — even though they haven't fully developed yet.

Think of it this way: a seed holds the promise of a tree. The tree doesn't exist yet, but the potential is clearly there.

This meaning is about possibility and potential, not commitment. No one is making a vow here. The word is simply being used to say: "the signs look good."

Examples:

"The young musician shows great promise."
(= She has early signs of becoming excellent. She may be outstanding one day.)

"This new treatment holds promise for patients with the disease."
(= Early results suggest it may work very well.)

"The morning felt full of promise."
(= It seemed like it was going to be a wonderful day — the signs were good.)

"There is little promise in that idea."
(= It doesn't seem like it will lead anywhere good.)

"A promising start" — though this uses the adjective form, it captures the same idea: an early phase that suggests good things are coming.

Common phrases in this sense

Show promise — to display clear potential; often used for people, especially young ones
"Her teachers said she showed tremendous promise from a very young age."

Hold promise — to suggest good future outcomes; slightly more formal, often used for ideas, plans, treatments, technologies
"The new approach holds great promise for renewable energy."

Full of promise — having lots of potential; often used to describe a situation, a moment, or a person's early stage
"Those were years full of promise, before things went wrong."

A promise of things to come — an early sign that something even better is ahead
"That performance was just a promise of things to come."
How to tell which meaning is being used

Context almost always makes it immediately clear.

If the sentence involves a person committing to do something for or to another person — it is Meaning 1 (a commitment).

If the sentence is about someone or something showing potential — it is Meaning 2 (potential).

Compare:

  • "His promise to repay me" → Meaning 1 (he committed to paying me back)
  • "His work shows promise" → Meaning 2 (his work has potential)

One quick test: ask yourself, "Is someone making a commitment to someone here?" If yes, Meaning 1. If no, Meaning 2.
The deeper idea behind both meanings

Interestingly, both meanings of promise share something in common: they both point toward the future, and they both carry a sense of confident expectation. In Meaning 1, a person confidently commits that something will happen. In Meaning 2, early signs confidently suggest that something could happen. The word promise, in both its uses, is fundamentally about what the future holds.

That is the word promise — in full.
12869:
A promontory is a high, raised piece of land that juts out boldly into a body of water — such as a sea, ocean, or lake — or that rises dramatically above the lower land around it. Think of it as nature's pointing finger: a solid, elevated landmass that pushes forward and stands out from everything surrounding it.

Two qualities define a promontory above all else: it is elevated (higher than the ground or water around it), and it projects outward (it extends forward, beyond the general line of the coast or landscape).

Picture yourself standing on a beach. You look to one side and see a large, rocky mass of land — steep, high, and cliff-like — pushing out boldly into the sea like a giant arm reaching into the water. Ships have to navigate carefully around it. Seabirds nest on its rocky face. A lighthouse is sometimes built at its very tip because it extends so far out, giving a sweeping view of the open water. That is a promontory.
Can a promontory exist away from water?

Yes, though this is less common. The word can also describe a high ridge or raised mass of land that stands out prominently above the lower terrain around it — even without any water nearby. A steep rocky outcrop jutting out from a hillside, for instance, can correctly be called a promontory.
How it differs from similar words

These words are close cousins, and mixing them up is easy, so it's worth being precise:

A cape is also a piece of land that extends into water, but it doesn't have to be high or elevated — it can be low and flat. A promontory is always high.

A headland is very nearly the same thing as a promontory, and the two are often used interchangeably. Both refer to a high point of land jutting into the sea. If there's any practical difference, "headland" is slightly more everyday and informal, while "promontory" carries a more formal and literary weight.

A peninsula is a large stretch of land surrounded by water on three sides (think of Italy or Florida). A promontory is typically much smaller and specifically refers to a bold, high, forward-jutting landform. A promontory can exist at the tip of a peninsula, but a full peninsula is a much broader geographic feature, not necessarily elevated.

A cliff is a steep, vertical rock face — a wall of rock. A promontory may have cliffs on its sides, but the promontory is the entire elevated landform projecting outward, not just the rock face itself.
The tone and register of the word

"Promontory" is not a word you'd casually drop into everyday conversation. It belongs to formal writing, geography, history, and especially literature and poetry. Because the landform itself is dramatic — high, exposed, thrusting into the sea — the word naturally carries a sense of grandeur and power. Writers reach for it when they want to paint a picture of wild, sweeping, imposing landscape.

• "The old lighthouse stood alone at the tip of the promontory, with nothing but open sea stretching to the horizon."
  • "From the promontory, we could see the entire bay spread out below us like a map."
  • "The castle had been built on a promontory, making it easy to defend — enemies could only attack from one direction."
  • "The ship rounded the promontory carefully, its captain wary of the hidden rocks below."
  • "He climbed to the top of the rocky promontory and watched the storm roll in from the west."

A promontory is a high, prominent piece of land — usually rocky — that juts out into a sea, lake, or river, or that rises steeply above lower surrounding terrain; it is the same idea as a headland, but more formal and literary in feel, and it is always elevated, unlike a flat cape.
